name: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate
lead: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD ascorbate, THDA) is an oil-soluble ester derivative of vitamin C used in serums and moisturisers marketed for brightening and anti-ageing. It is used as an alternative to L-ascorbic acid, which is described as unstable and sometimes irritating at high concentrations [1][2]. Vitamin C products are used with the aim of evening skin tone, fading dark spots and softening the look of sun-related ageing, and an oil-soluble ester is one way formulators try to deliver it in a gentler, more stable form.

Human data on THDA specifically are limited to small, mostly manufacturer-associated studies of multi-ingredient products. A 2021 laboratory study reported that it degrades rapidly under oxidative stress but can be stabilised by acetyl zingerone [3], and a 2024 randomized double-blind study compared THDA with and without acetyl zingerone on facial photoaging [4].

Formulators describe THDA as lipid-soluble with skin-mimicking properties, and a 2026 trial report characterised it as having superior stability compared with ascorbic acid [15]. A 2026 systematic review of vitamin C in dermatology described THDA as preferred for sensitive skin in the literature it covered, while noting it needs stabilisation with acetyl zingerone [14].

paras: THDA is an ascorbic acid ester designed to dissolve in oils, in contrast to water-soluble L-ascorbic acid. Vitamin C in general is described as labile, with oxidation accelerated by light, oxygen, heat and higher pH [5]. Studies of vitamin C in skin care frame delivery and instability as the main formulation challenges [2].

Wikipedia's vitamin C article describes ascorbic acid as the form that gives the vitamin its biological activity, and notes that its oxidation is accelerated by light, oxygen, heat and higher pH, which is the background to the search for derivatives such as THDA.[5] Reviews of vitamin C in skin care describe L-ascorbic acid as effective in studies but demanding to formulate, with low pH and high concentration needed for delivery, and irritation reported by some users.[2][1]

sections.h: Role of vitamin C in skin
paras: Vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, a step that lets collagen form a stable triple helix [5]. This biochemistry is the reason topical vitamin C is used in anti-ageing products: collagen in the dermis underlies firmness and fine-line appearance. Vitamin C is also an antioxidant, which is the basis for its use against UV- and light-induced oxidative stress, and in vitro work indicates it can reduce melanin production, the basis for brightening claims [15].

Several derivatives exist beside THDA. Ascorbyl palmitate, a fatty acid ester of vitamin C, is used both in cosmetics and as a food antioxidant [5]. The 2026 systematic review, covering 44 studies from 2020 onward, described L-ascorbic acid as the most clinically validated form, with low-pH stabilised systems and combinations with vitamin E and ferulic acid improving photoaging and pigmentary disorders; it described ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate as having superior lipophilic stability, ascorbyl glucoside as well tolerated for chronic hyperpigmentation, and THDA as preferred for sensitive skin but requiring acetyl zingerone stabilisation [14].

The studies below test products or regimens containing THDA and cannot attribute effects to it alone. A prospective open-label, evaluator-blinded study of a dual regimen including a 30% vitamin C formulation reported lightening of facial melasma over a summer [2]. Open-label trials of multi-ingredient regimens combining retinol and vitamin C, and of an anti-ageing moisturiser, reported improvements in hyperpigmentation and photodamage appearance [6][7]. A hydroquinone-free brightening product was assessed through melanogenesis inhibition in vitro and UV-induced hyperpigmentation in people [8]. A multicorrective product was assessed for dark circles and puffiness [9].

A 2026 randomized double-blind trial report evaluated a serum containing 30% THD ascorbate in a patent-pending blend of antioxidants and prebiotics, on hyperpigmented and photodamaged skin. In an in vitro tissue model exposed to blue light, the serum reduced reactive oxygen species formation by 88% at 30 minutes, and melanin production fell by 24% in a tissue co-culture; the abstract also reports improvements in skin structure [15].

An older double-blind half-face study applied a complex of 10% ascorbic acid and 7% THD ascorbate in an anhydrous gel to one side of the face of ten patients, and the vehicle to the other, assessing wrinkling, pigmentation, inflammation and hydration at 4, 8 and 12 weeks, with biopsies in four patients [11]. That study is a small one and its preparation contained both vitamin C forms.

THDA appears in serums, eye products and moisturisers marketed for brightening and photoageing, usually alongside other ingredients such as retinol, niacinamide or acetyl zingerone.[6][7][4][9] Product evaluations in the published literature measure outcomes such as hyperpigmentation scores, wrinkle ratings and dark-circle appearance over several weeks to months.[6][7][9] Because most tested products contain several actives, the studies describe the effect of the regimen, not of THDA alone.[2][6]

A 2021 study reported that THDA degrades rapidly under oxidative stress but could be stabilised by acetyl zingerone, with enhanced collagen production and antioxidant effects in vitro [3]. Acetyl zingerone is described as a photostable ingredient [10].

Vitamin C derivatives are often chosen by people whose skin reacts to L-ascorbic acid, and THDA is described as preferred for sensitive skin [14]. Allergic reactions to it have nevertheless been documented: a 2022 report in Contact Dermatitis described allergic contact dermatitis to two eye creams containing THDA [16]. Acetyl zingerone, the stabiliser used alongside it, has been described as possibly blunting pro-inflammatory effects of THDA such as activation of type I interferon signalling [10].

A 2024 prospective randomized double-blind comparative study examined topical acetyl zingerone with THDA versus THDA alone on facial photoaging [4]. An earlier double-blind half-face study tested a topical vitamin C preparation against vehicle for photodamage, though the abstract does not identify THDA as the test form [11]. Registered trials include an eye-serum study (n=35) for the periorbital area and an AI-personalised regimen study for photoaging in women (n=43) [12][13]. Many of these were run or supported by companies that make the products.

The 2026 randomized trial of a 30% THDA serum and the 2002 half-face study both used products in which THDA was one component, and the 2026 report describes a double-blind design with accompanying laboratory models [15][11].

card.summary: An oil-soluble vitamin C ester for serums; human data come from small, product-level studies.
card.note: Trials test multi-ingredient products and are often company-linked.

quick.overview:
Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate is a fat-soluble form of vitamin C used in brightening and anti-ageing serums, positioned as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid.
Studies are small and test whole regimens, so its own effect is not isolated.
quick.mechanism: As an ascorbate ester it is used as an antioxidant and pigment-modulating vitamin C source; lab work shows it can degrade under oxidative stress unless stabilised.
quick.risks: Trials of products containing it report generally good tolerance; no specific serious safety signals were found.
